sentences.t:
oð ðæt hīe forlǣddan tō ðām lindplegan
swǣse gesīðas ond hyra sylfra feorh.
sentences.l: until they led to ruin, to the linden-play, dear companions and their own lives.
sentences.i: until they brought their dear companions, and their own lives, to ruin in the shield-play.
sentences.n: Klaeber prints the section numeral [XXVIIII–XXX] at line 2039 (the manuscript skips a number) and marks no break at 2093; the division at 2093 is ours. The manuscript marks the new canto only with a large capital ‘O’, which is the first letter of ‘oð’. This is the middle of a sentence begun in the last part, where the Heathobards could wield the heirloom weapons of the old men ‘þenden’ (‘while’; 2036–2038), and ‘oð ðæt’ (‘until’) ends that time. Beowulf is speaking to Higelāc, foretelling how the Danish marriage will go wrong. ‘forlǣddan’ is the plural past of ‘forlǣdan’, ‘lead astray, lead to ruin’. ‘swǣse gesīðas’ (‘dear companions’) and ‘hyra sylfra feorh’ (‘their own lives’; ‘hyra’ and ‘sylfra’ are both genitive plural) are its objects. ‘lindplega’ is ‘linden-play’, battle: linden-wood made the shield.

sentences.t:
Þonne cwið æt bēore sē ðe bēah gesyhð,
eald æscwiga, sē ðe eall gem(an),
gārcwealm gumena — him bið grim sefa —,
sentences.l: Then says at beer he who sees the ring, the old ash-warrior, he who remembers all, the spear-death of men — grim is his mind —,
sentences.i: Then at the beer an old spear-warrior will speak, one who sees the ring and remembers it all, the spear-slaughter of men — his mind is grim —
sentences.n: ‘cwið’ is the present tense of ‘cweðan’, ‘say’, and here a present for the future: Beowulf is describing what will happen. ‘sē ðe’ is ‘he who’. ‘æscwiga’ is ‘ash-warrior’: ‘æsc’, ‘ash’, is the wood of a spear-shaft and so means a spear. ‘gem(an)’ is the present of ‘gemunan’, ‘remember’, and the letters in parentheses are restored where the manuscript is fire-damaged; Klaeber follows Thorkelin’s ‘an’, and Grundtvig’s transcript has ‘on’. Its object is ‘gārcwealm gumena’, ‘the spear-death of men’ (‘gār’ ‘spear’, ‘cwealm’ ‘death’). ‘him bið grim sefa’ is ‘to him is a grim mind’, set off by dashes. ‘bēah gesyhð’, ‘sees the ring’, is unclear: the ring is not named. I guess a ring on the sword or its fittings that the old man sees on the young Dane, but Grein suggested ‘bill’ (sword) in place of ‘bēah’, Bugge ‘bā’, and Holthausen and Sedgefield ‘beorn’ (warrior), so the word is doubtful.

sentences.t:
onginneð geōmormōd geong(um) cempan
þurh hreðra gehygd higes cunnian,
wīgbealu weccean, ond þæt word ācwyð:
sentences.l: begins, sad-minded, to the young warrior, through the thought of the breasts, of the mind to make trial, war-evil to wake, and that word utters:
sentences.i: Sorrowful at heart, he sets about testing the young warrior’s spirit, out of what he thinks in his breast, to stir up the evil of war; and he speaks these words:
sentences.n: ‘onginneð’ is a second main verb, ‘begins’, with the infinitives ‘cunnian’ (‘to test’) and ‘weccean’ (‘to wake’); ‘cunnian’ takes a genitive, ‘higes’, ‘of the mind’. ‘geōmormōd’, ‘sad-minded’, is a nominative describing the old man. The (um) of ‘geong(um) cempan’ is restored (the manuscript is damaged) and the dative ‘to the young warrior’ is Kemble’s reading; Grundtvig’s transcript and Schücking restore ‘geong(ne)’, an accusative, ‘the young warrior’, which would make him a direct object instead of the one addressed. ‘hreðra’ is the genitive plural of ‘hreðer’, ‘breast’, a poetic plural, and ‘gehygd’ is ‘thought’, so ‘through’ here is ‘out of’. ‘wīgbealu’, ‘war-evil’, is the feud itself. ‘ācwyð’ is ‘utters’, from ‘ācweðan’. Klaeber’s colon begins the old man’s speech.

sentences.t:
“Meaht ðū, mīn wine, mēce gecnāwan,
þone þīn fæder tō gefeohte bær
under heregrīman hindeman sīðe,
dȳre īren,
sentences.l: “Can you, my friend, know the sword, which your father to the fight bore, under the army-mask on the last journey, the dear iron,
sentences.i: “Can you, my friend, recognise the sword that your father carried into the fight, helmed for war, on his last venture — that precious iron —
sentences.n: ‘Meaht ðū’ is ‘can you’, with the verb first as in a question: ‘meaht’ is the second-person present of ‘magan’. ‘mīn wine’ is ‘my friend’, a vocative. ‘mēce’ is the accusative of ‘mēce’, ‘sword’, the object of ‘gecnāwan’, ‘recognise’; ‘þone’ (‘which’) points back to it, and ‘dȳre īren’, ‘dear iron’, is the same sword said again, ‘īren’ standing for the blade. ‘under heregrīman’ is ‘under the army-mask’: ‘here’ is ‘army, war-host’ and ‘grīma’ ‘mask’, here a helmet. ‘hindeman sīðe’ is a dative of time, ‘on the last journey’ or ‘for the last time’ (‘sīð’ is both ‘journey’ and ‘time’), ‘hindeman’ being ‘hindmost’. The speaker is an old Heathobard and the ‘you’ is a young Heathobard whose father fell in an earlier fight with the Danes; the sword he is asked about is on the young Dane in the hall.

sentences.t:
þǣr hyne Dene slōgon,
wēoldon wælstōwe, syððan Wiðergyld læg,
æfter hæleþa hryre, hwate Scyldungas?
sentences.l: where him Danes slew, held the slaughter-place, after Wiðergyld lay, after the heroes’ fall, the bold Scyldings?
sentences.i: where the Danes killed him — the bold Scyldings, who held the field of slaughter after Wiðergyld lay dead and the heroes had fallen?
sentences.n: ‘þǣr hyne Dene slōgon’ is ‘where the Danes slew him’: ‘hyne’ is the accusative ‘him’, the father, and ‘Dene’ a nominative plural. ‘wēoldon wælstōwe’ is ‘held the place of slaughter’: ‘wealdan’ takes a dative, ‘wælstōwe’, and holding the field meant winning the battle. ‘hwate Scyldungas’ is ‘the bold Scyldings’, the Danes again: ‘Scyldungas’ means descendants of Scyld, as ‘Scyldingas’ does. ‘syððan Wiðergyld læg’ is ‘after Wiðergyld lay’. Wiðergyld is named only here, and I take him to be a Heathobard killed in the same fight, but that is a guess from the context. ‘æfter hæleþa hryre’ is ‘after the heroes’ fall’. The question mark ends the question begun at 2047.

sentences.t:
Nū hēr þāra banena byre nāthwylces
frætwum hrēmig on flet gæ̂ð,
sentences.l: Now here, of those slayers, of I-know-not-which, the son, exulting in trappings, onto the floor goes,
sentences.i: Now here, the son of one or other of those who slew him goes about the hall exulting in his finery,
sentences.n: ‘þāra banena’ is ‘of those slayers’, a genitive plural of ‘bana’ (cf. ‘bona’), the men who killed your father. ‘nāthwylces’ is a genitive going with ‘þāra banena’, ‘of some one of those slayers’: ‘nāthwylc’ is from ‘ne wāt hwylc’, ‘I do not know which’, a scornful ‘some one or other’. ‘byre’ is the nominative ‘son’, a singular since ‘gæ̂ð’ is singular. ‘frætwum hrēmig’ is ‘exulting in trappings’, the dative ‘frætwum’ following ‘hrēmig’; compare ‘hūðe hrēmig’ at 124. ‘on flet gæ̂ð’ is ‘goes onto the hall-floor’, ‘flet’ being the floor of the hall; the circumflex is Klaeber’s contraction mark, as at 2034. This is the young Dane, seen by the old man as the heir of a killer.

sentences.t:
morðres gylpeð, ond þone māðþum byreð,
þone þe ðū mid rihte rǣdan sceoldest.”
sentences.l: of murder he boasts, and the treasure bears, which you by right ought to rule.”
sentences.i: He boasts of the murder, and carries the treasure that by right you should possess.”
sentences.n: ‘morðres gylpeð’ is ‘boasts of murder’: ‘gylpan’ takes a genitive, ‘morðres’. The manuscript has ‘gylped’, and Kemble made it ‘gylpeð’. ‘māðþum’ is ‘treasure’, here the sword, and ‘byreð’ is ‘bears’, the third-person present of ‘beran’, with the mutated vowel (‘byreð’ for ‘bereð’); I take ‘bears’ to mean ‘wears at his side’. ‘þone þe ðū mid rihte rǣdan sceoldest’ is ‘which you by right ought to rule’: ‘rǣdan’ is ‘have the ordering of, hold’, ‘sceoldest’ the second-person past of ‘sculan’, ‘ought’, and ‘mid rihte’ ‘with right’. The inheritance is the old man’s argument: the sword belongs to the son of the man it was taken from. The closing quotation mark ends the speech.

sentences.t:
Manað swā ond myndgað mǣla gehwylce
sārum wordum, oð ðæt sǣl cymeð,
sentences.l: He urges so and reminds at every time, with sore words, until the time comes,
sentences.i: So he goads him, and reminds him at every occasion with bitter words, until the time comes
sentences.n: ‘Manað’ and ‘myndgað’ are the third-person present of ‘manian’, ‘urge’, and ‘myndgian’, ‘remind’; the object ‘him’ is left to be understood. ‘mǣla gehwylce’ is ‘at every time’, ‘mǣl’ being ‘time, occasion’, and ‘sārum wordum’ is ‘with sore words’, a dative of means. ‘oð ðæt sǣl cymeð’ is ‘until the time comes’: ‘sǣl’ with a long vowel is ‘time, good occasion’. The speech is over and Beowulf now tells what the speech will lead to, in his own voice.

sentences.l: that the woman’s thane, for his father’s deeds, after the blade’s bite, blood-stained sleeps, guilty of life;
sentences.i: when the bride’s thane, for what his father did, lies sleeping, bloodstained, after the bite of a blade, forfeit of his life;
sentences.n: ‘þæt’ is the conjunction ‘that’, and here it names what the ‘time’ will bring. ‘fǣmnan þegn’ is ‘the woman’s thane’, ‘fǣmnan’ being the genitive of ‘fǣmne’, ‘woman, maiden’; Barnouw prints it as one compound word (Klaeber refers to his own note on 910 f.). It is disputed who this is. I take it to be the Danish retainer who came with the bride (the retinue at 2034–2035), who now pays for what his father did. ‘fore fæder dǣdum’ is ‘for father’s deeds’, ‘fæder’ a genitive singular and ‘dǣdum’ a dative plural. ‘æfter billes bite’ is ‘after the sword’s bite’. ‘blōdfāg’ is ‘blood-stained’ (‘fāg’, ‘stained’; ‘fǣge’ at 2077 is ‘doomed’), and ‘swefeð’ is ‘sleeps’, the usual soft word for lying dead. ‘ealdres scyldig’ is ‘guilty of life’: ‘scyldig’ takes a genitive and means ‘guilty of, forfeit of’, so the Dane has lost his life; the semicolon after it ends the clause.

sentences.t:
him se ōðer þonan
losað (li)figende, con him land geare.
sentences.l: for himself the other from there escapes, living, knows for himself the land well.
sentences.i: and the other slips away from there alive, for he knows the country well.
sentences.n: ‘se ōðer’ is ‘the other’, the young Heathobard, and the first ‘him’ is a dative of interest, ‘for himself’ (it could also be ‘from him’, the dead man). ‘losað’ is the third-person present of ‘losian’, which the lexica give as ‘be lost, perish’ but which seems to mean ‘get away’ here; that sense is a guess from the context. The (li) of ‘(li)figende’ is restored: the manuscript has ‘figende’, and Heyne’s second edition supplied ‘li’, ‘living’. ‘con him land geare’ is a crux. I read ‘con’ as ‘knows’ (‘cunnan’), ‘him’ as ‘for himself’, and ‘geare’ as an adverb, ‘well’, but the line has been read in other ways.

sentences.t:
Þonne bīoð (āb)rocene on bā healfe
āðsweord eorla;
sentences.l: Then are broken on both sides the oath-swords of earls;
sentences.i: Then the oaths of the earls are broken on both sides,
sentences.n: ‘bīoð’ is a form of ‘bēon’, ‘will be’, and ‘(āb)rocene’ is the past participle of ‘ābrecan’, ‘break’. The letters in parentheses are restored: the manuscript has ‘orocene’ in one copy and ‘.orocene’ in the other, and Kemble supplied ‘āb’, while Thorkelin and Schücking read ‘brocene’. ‘on bā healfe’ is ‘on both sides’. ‘āðsweord’ is a crux. The compound would be ‘oath-sword’ (‘āð’ ‘oath’, ‘sweord’ ‘sword’) and occurs only here; Klaeber’s italic ‘d’ shows that he altered the manuscript, which has ‘sweorð’ (a doubtful reading), after Thorkelin’s ‘-sweord’. I guess it means the oaths sworn on swords, which fits ‘ābrocene’; ‘oath-swords’ in the literal line is only the parts of the word. ‘eorla’ is a genitive plural, ‘of earls’, and ‘āðsweord’ a neuter plural (‘sweord’ has no plural ending), the subject of ‘bīoð’. Both sides break their oaths.

sentences.t:
(syð)ðan Ingelde
weallað wælnīðas, ond him wīflufan
æfter cearwælmum cōlran weorðað.
sentences.l: after that, for Ingeld, slaughter-hatreds well up, and for him the wife-loves after care-surges become cooler.
sentences.i: After that, deadly hatreds boil up in Ingeld, and after the surges of his sorrow his love for his wife grows cooler.
sentences.n: ‘(syð)ðan’ is ‘after that’, the first letters restored by Kemble. ‘Ingelde’ is a dative, ‘in Ingeld’ or ‘for Ingeld’: the name appears here for the first time, and he is the Heathobard bridegroom, the son of Froda (2025). ‘weallað’ is the plural present of ‘weallan’, ‘boil, well up’, with the subject ‘wælnīðas’, ‘slaughter-hatreds’ (‘wæl’ ‘slaughter’, ‘nīð’ ‘hatred’). ‘him’ is a dative, ‘for him’. ‘wīflufan’ is ‘wife-loves’, a plural for ‘love of his wife’, and ‘cearwælmum’ ‘care-surges’ (‘wælm’ ‘surge, welling’), a dative plural after ‘æfter’. ‘cōlran’ is the comparative ‘cooler’ and ‘weorðað’ ‘become’. So the marriage arranged to end the feud brings it back.

sentences.t:
Þȳ ic Heaðo-Bear[d]na hyldo ne telge,
dryhtsibbe dǣl Denum unfǣcne,
frēondscipe fæstne.
sentences.l: Therefore I the Heathobards’ favour do not reckon, the share of lord-kinship to the Danes unfalse, friendship firm.
sentences.i: And so I do not count the Heathobards’ goodwill, or their share in the bond between the lords, as true to the Danes, nor their friendship as firm.
sentences.n: ‘Þȳ’ is ‘therefore’, an instrumental. ‘telge’ is the first-person present of ‘tellan’, here ‘reckon, count’. ‘hyldo’ is ‘favour, loyalty’, an accusative, and the Heathobards’ name is ‘Heaðo-Bear[d]na’, a genitive plural; Klaeber adds the ‘d’, since the manuscript has ‘bearna’ (‘of the children’) and Thorkelin supplied ‘-beardna’. The line is a crux. I take ‘hyldo’, ‘dryhtsibbe dǣl’ (‘share of lord-kinship’) and ‘frēondscipe’ as objects of ‘telge’, with ‘unfǣcne’ (‘unfalse’) and ‘fæstne’ (‘firm’) saying what Beowulf does not count them to be, and ‘Denum’ a dative, ‘to the Danes’. That is a guess at a very compressed sentence, and some editors read it otherwise. ‘dryhtsibb’ is peace between lords made by marriage.

sentences.t:
Ic sceal forð sprecan
gēn ymbe Grendel, þæt ðū geare cunne,
sinces brytta, tō hwan syððan wearð
hondrǣs hæleða.
sentences.l: I shall forth speak still about Grendel, that you well may know, dispenser of treasure, to what thereafter came the hand-rush of heroes.
sentences.i: I must go on speaking about Grendel, giver of treasure, so that you may know well what came of the hand-to-hand clash of the men.
sentences.n: Beowulf leaves the Heathobards. ‘Ic sceal forð sprecan’ is ‘I shall speak forth’, ‘sceal’ meaning ‘must’ or simply ‘shall’; ‘gēn’ is ‘still, further’, ‘ymbe’ ‘about’ (Grein and Holthausen print ‘ymb’), and ‘Grendel’ the object of it. ‘þæt ðū geare cunne’ is ‘that you may know well’, ‘cunne’ a subjunctive of ‘cunnan’. ‘sinces brytta’ is ‘dispenser of treasure’, a vocative: Higelāc, as at 1170, where Wealhtheow so addresses Hrothgar. ‘tō hwan … wearð’ is ‘what became of’, ‘hwan’ an instrumental of ‘hwā’. ‘hondrǣs’ is ‘hand-rush’, the clash of hand to hand, and ‘hæleða’ a genitive plural, ‘of heroes’; the fight is Beowulf’s with Grendel.

sentences.t:
Syððan heofones gim
glād ofer grundas, gǣst yrre cwōm,
eatol ǣfengrom ūser nēosan,
ðǣr wē gesunde sæl weardodon.
sentences.l: After heaven’s gem glided over the grounds, the spirit came, angry, dire, evening-fierce, to seek us out, where we, sound, guarded the hall.
sentences.i: After the sun had glided over the lands, the angry spirit came, dire and fierce in the evening, to seek us out, where we, unharmed, were keeping the hall.
sentences.n: ‘heofones gim’ is ‘heaven’s gem’, a kenning for the sun: ‘syððan … glād’ gives the time, ‘after it had glided’. ‘grundas’ are ‘grounds’, the lands. ‘gǣst yrre cwōm’ is ‘the angry spirit came’; ‘gǣst’ I take as a spelling of ‘gāst’, ‘spirit’, and ‘yrre’ is ‘angry’. ‘eatol ǣfengrom’ is ‘dire, evening-fierce’, ‘ǣfengrom’ being ‘ǣfen’ (‘evening’) and ‘grom’ (‘fierce’), a word found only here. ‘ūser’ is a genitive, ‘of us’, as ‘nēosan’, ‘to seek out’, takes the genitive. ‘ðǣr’ is ‘where’, and ‘sæl weardodon’ is ‘guarded the hall’: ‘sæl’ with a short vowel is ‘hall’ (it is ‘sele’), a different word from the ‘sǣl’ of 2058, with its long vowel. ‘gesunde’ is ‘sound, safe’.

sentences.l: There was to Hondsciô battle, a falling-on, life-bale to the doomed; he first lay, the girded champion;
sentences.i: There battle fell upon Hondscio, deadly harm for a doomed man; he was the first to lie dead, a belted warrior;
sentences.n: ‘Hondsciô’ is a dative, ‘to Hondscio’: the circumflex is Klaeber’s contraction mark, and the name seems to be ‘hond’ (‘hand’) and ‘scōh’ (‘shoe’), a glove; whether the poet means a play on the glove of 2085 is only a guess. ‘hild’ is the subject; the manuscript has ‘hilde’ and Holtzmann and Rieger read ‘hild’, which Klaeber follows (his italic ‘d’). ‘onsǣge’ is rare, taken as ‘a falling-upon, an attack’ (a guess; the lexica give it as an adjective ‘attacking’). ‘feorhbealu fǣgum’ is ‘life-bale to the doomed’, ‘fǣgum’ a dative of ‘fǣge’, ‘doomed to die’. ‘fyrmest’ is ‘first’, and ‘gyrded cempa’ ‘girded champion’, a man belted with his sword. This is the first time the poem names the victim.

sentences.t:
him Grendel wearð,
mǣrum maguþegne tō mūðbonan,
sentences.l: to him Grendel became, to the famed young thane, a mouth-slayer,
sentences.i: Grendel became his slayer, the slayer of that famed young retainer, a killer with his mouth —
sentences.n: ‘him … wearð … tō mūðbonan’ is ‘became to him a mouth-slayer’: ‘wearð’ is the past of ‘weorðan’, ‘become’, ‘tō’ with a dative says what Grendel became, and ‘him’ is the dative, ‘to him’. ‘mūðbona’ is ‘mouth-slayer’ (‘mūð’ ‘mouth’, ‘bona’ ‘slayer’), a compound known only here: Grendel kills by eating. ‘mǣrum maguþegne’ is ‘to the famed young thane’, a dative apposed to ‘him’: ‘mǣrum’ is ‘famed’; ‘maguþegne’ has an italic ‘u’ because the manuscript has ‘magū’ and Kemble made it ‘magu-’; ‘magu’ is ‘young man, son’, so ‘maguþegn’ is a young retainer. The sleeper eaten at 740–745 has no name there; Hondscio is named only here.

sentences.t: lēofes mannes līc eall forswealg.
sentences.l: of the dear man the body all he swallowed up.
sentences.i: He swallowed up the whole body of the beloved man.
sentences.n: ‘lēofes mannes līc’ is ‘the dear man’s body’, with ‘lēofes mannes’ a genitive and ‘līc’ the accusative object of ‘forswealg’, the past of ‘forswelgan’, ‘swallow up’, the prefix ‘for-’ making it thorough. ‘eall’ is ‘all, entirely’. The eating was told at 740–745, where Grendel ‘swealh’ a sleeping man and had eaten all of him, ‘fēt ond folma’, ‘feet and hands’ too; Beowulf now says it briefly. ‘lēof’ is ‘dear’.

sentences.l: Not the sooner out then yet empty-handed the slayer, blood-toothed, mindful of evils, from the gold-hall go would;
sentences.i: Yet the blood-toothed slayer, with evil on his mind, would not for that go out of the gold-hall empty-handed any sooner;
sentences.n: ‘Nō ðȳ ǣr’ is ‘none the sooner’: ‘ðȳ’ an instrumental, ‘ǣr’ ‘earlier’. ‘ūt … gongan wolde’ is ‘would go out’, ‘wolde’ meaning ‘was willing’, so ‘would not … go’. ‘gēn’ is ‘still, yet’, and ‘īdelhende’ is ‘empty-handed’ (‘īdel’ ‘empty’, ‘hand’ ‘hand’). ‘bona blōdigtōð’ is ‘slayer, blood-toothed’: ‘bona’ is a nominative, Grendel, and ‘blōdigtōð’ is a compound of ‘blōdig’ and ‘tōð’, ‘tooth’. ‘bealewa gemyndig’ is ‘mindful of evils’: ‘gemyndig’ takes the genitive, ‘bealewa’ (a plural of ‘bealu’, ‘evil, harm’), meaning either intent on harming or remembering the harm done to him; I cannot tell which. ‘goldsele’ is ‘gold-hall’, Heorot.

sentences.t:
ac hē mægnes rōf mīn costode,
grāpode gearofolm.
sentences.l: but he, bold of might, made trial of me, grasped, ready-handed.
sentences.i: Instead, bold and strong as he was, he put me to the test and grasped with ready hand.
sentences.n: ‘ac’ is ‘but’, and Grendel is still ‘hē’. ‘mægnes rōf’ is ‘bold of strength’, ‘mægnes’ a genitive of respect. ‘mīn costode’ is ‘tried me’: ‘costian’ takes the genitive, and ‘mīn’ is the genitive of ‘ic’, ‘of me’. ‘grāpode’ is the past of ‘grāpian’, ‘grasp’, and ‘gearofolm’ is ‘ready-handed’ (‘gearo’ ‘ready’, ‘folm’ ‘hand’), a nominative describing Grendel. Klaeber’s italic ‘o’ marks a change: the manuscript has ‘geareo’, Thorkelin printed ‘gearo’, and Kemble’s second edition ‘gearo-’, which Klaeber follows.

sentences.t:
Glōf hangode
sīd ond syllīc, searobendum fæst;
sentences.l: A glove hung, broad and wondrous, fast with cunning-bonds;
sentences.i: A glove hung, broad and wondrous, made fast with cunning bonds;
sentences.n: ‘Glōf’ is ‘glove’, a feminine noun, so the ‘sīo’ of the next line is ‘it’. ‘hangode’ is ‘hung’. ‘sīd’ is ‘broad, ample’ and ‘syllīc’ ‘wondrous, strange’, both describing the glove, so the glove would have been a large pouch or bag; that is an inference. ‘searobendum fæst’ is ‘fast with cunning-bonds’: ‘searu’ is ‘skill, craft’ and ‘bend’ ‘bond’, the dative plural after ‘fæst’. No other part of the poem mentions this glove, so everything said of it comes from this passage.

sentences.t:
sīo wæs orðoncum eall gegyrwed
dēofles cræftum ond dracan fellum.
sentences.l: it was with cunning-devices all prepared by the devil’s crafts and with a dragon’s skins.
sentences.i: It was all fitted out with ingenious devices, by the devil’s crafts and with dragon skins.
sentences.n: ‘sīo’ is the feminine ‘it’, the glove. ‘gegyrwed’ is ‘prepared, fitted out’, the past participle of ‘gegyrwan’. ‘orðoncum’ is a crux: ‘orðanc’ means ‘skill, cunning, device’, here in a dative plural ‘with ingenious devices’; the word is rare and the sense is the lexica’s. ‘dēofles cræftum’ is ‘by the devil’s crafts’, a genitive ‘dēofles’ and a dative ‘cræftum’, and ‘dracan fellum’ ‘with dragon skins’ (‘dracan’ a genitive singular), ‘fell’ being a hide. The manuscript has ‘ond’ before ‘dracan’; Trautmann’s ‘of’ would give ‘made by the devil’s crafts of dragon skins’, which fits ‘gegyrwed’; Klaeber keeps ‘ond’.

sentences.l: He me there within, sinless, the fierce deed-doer, to put wanted, one of many;
sentences.i: That fierce doer of deeds meant to put me in there, guiltless as I was, as one among many;
sentences.n: ‘Hē’ is Grendel, and ‘mec’ is an older form of ‘mē’, accusative ‘me’. ‘þǣr on innan’ is ‘there within’, into the glove. ‘unsynnigne’ is ‘sinless, guiltless’, an accusative describing ‘mec’. ‘dīor dǣdfruma’ is ‘fierce deed-doer’ (‘dǣd’ ‘deed’, ‘fruma’ ‘beginner, doer’), ‘dīor’ being a spelling of ‘dēor’, ‘fierce’, which also means ‘brave’ or ‘dear’, here in the fierce sense. ‘gedōn wolde’ is ‘wished to put’, and ‘manigra sumne’ is ‘one of many’, the accusative ‘sumne’ with a genitive plural. The glove was to hold the men he took, one after another.

sentences.t:
hyt ne mihte swā,
syððan ic on yrre uppriht āstōd.
sentences.l: it could not so, after I in anger upright stood up.
sentences.i: It could not be so, once I had stood upright in my anger.
sentences.n: ‘hyt’ is ‘it’, the plan; ‘ne mihte swā’ is ‘could not (be) so’, with the verb of being understood. ‘syððan’ is ‘after, once’, and ‘uppriht āstōd’ is ‘stood upright’, ‘āstōd’ being the past of ‘āstandan’, ‘stand up’. ‘on yrre’ is ‘in anger’, a dative of ‘yrre’, ‘anger’. Klaeber’s full stop ends the sentence here, so our division at 2093 falls at a sentence end, though he marks no section there.
